# Tuning tidymodels in Databricks {background-image="assets/title-slide-white.png" background-size="1500px" background-color="white"}

90 minutes to 3, with one new argument

Edgar Ruiz \@ Posit

[linkedin.com/in/edgararuiz](https://www.linkedin.com/in/edgararuiz/)

# The problem {background-image="assets/slide-frame-dark.png" background-size="1500px" background-color="#2a7070"}

:::{.dark-slide}
Grid search is slow, and it is slow on your laptop
:::

## Grid search does a lot of fitting {background-image="assets/slide-frame.png" background-size="1500px" background-color="white"}

- Tuning a boosted tree with four parameters: `mtry`, `min_n`, `learn_rate`, `tree_depth`

- A space filling grid of **100 combinations**

- 10 fold cross validation

:::{.big-number}
1,000 model fits
:::

:::{.big-number-sub}
for one call to `tune_grid()`
:::

## The usual answers are not enough {background-image="assets/slide-frame.png" background-size="1500px" background-color="white"}

- Run it in parallel on your laptop, and you are still bound by the cores you own

- Move it to a server, and the server is often *slower* than the laptop

- Rewrite the model in Spark ML, and you leave tidymodels behind

- Meanwhile, the Databricks cluster your data already lives in sits idle

# The example {background-image="assets/slide-frame-dark.png" background-size="1500px" background-color="#2a7070"}

:::{.dark-slide}
Hospital readmissions, a plain tidymodels workflow
:::

## The setup {background-image="assets/slide-frame.png" background-size="1500px" background-color="white"}

:::{.sample-medium}
```r
library(tidymodels)
library(readmission)

set.seed(231)
readmission_splits <- initial_split(readmission, strata = readmitted)

readmission_folds <- vfold_cv(training(readmission_splits), strata = readmitted)

recipe_basic <- recipe(readmitted ~ ., data = training(readmission_splits)) |>
  step_mutate(
    race = factor(case_when(
      !(race %in% c("Caucasian", "African American")) ~ "Other",
      .default = race
    ))
  ) |>
  step_unknown(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_YeoJohnson(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())
```
:::

## The model and the grid {background-image="assets/slide-frame.png" background-size="1500px" background-color="white"}

:::{.sample-medium}
```r
spec_bt <- boost_tree(
  mode = "classification",
  trees = 500,
  mtry = tune(),
  min_n = tune(),
  learn_rate = tune(),
  tree_depth = tune()
)

bt_grid <- grid_space_filling(
  mtry(range = c(5, 20)),
  min_n(),
  learn_rate(),
  tree_depth(),
  size = 100
)
```
:::

## Tuning locally {background-image="assets/slide-frame.png" background-size="1500px" background-color="white"}

:::{.sample-medium}
```r
library(future)
plan(multisession)

local_results <- tune_grid(
  object = spec_bt,
  preprocessor = recipe_basic,
  resamples = readmission_folds,
  grid = bt_grid,
  control = control_grid()
)
```
:::

:::{.fragment .fade-in}
On an M3 laptop this takes **11 minutes**. On a Windows machine, **61 minutes**.
:::

# The feature {background-image="assets/slide-frame-dark.png" background-size="1500px" background-color="#2a7070"}

:::{.dark-slide}
`tune_grid_spark()`
:::

## One new argument {background-image="assets/slide-frame.png" background-size="1500px" background-color="white"}

:::{.sample-medium}
```r
library(sparklyr)

sc <- spark_connect(
  method = "databricks_connect",
  cluster_id = cluster_id
)

spark_results <- tune_grid_spark(
  sc = sc,                          # <- the only addition
  object = spec_bt,
  preprocessor = recipe_basic,
  resamples = readmission_folds,
  grid = bt_grid,
  control = control_grid(verbose = TRUE)
)
```
:::

- Same model spec, same recipe, same resamples, same grid

- Returns a regular `tune_results` object, so `collect_metrics()` and `select_best()` work as usual

## What happens under the hood {background-image="assets/slide-frame.png" background-size="1500px" background-color="white"}

- **Upload** - the resamples, model specification and preprocessing steps are serialized and sent to Databricks

- **Process** - each parameter combination is fitted on a worker, running real R through `reticulate` and `rpy2`

- **Collect** - the metrics come back and are assembled into a `tune_results` object

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  subgraph lp[Your machine]
    tm[tidymodels]
  end
  subgraph db[Databricks cluster]
    w1[R worker]
    w2[R worker]
    w3[R worker]
  end
  tm <-. objects / metrics .-> db

  style lp  fill:#fff,stroke:#666
  style db  fill:#f4c430,stroke:#666
  style tm  fill:#eff,stroke:#666
  style w1  fill:#fff,stroke:#666
  style w2  fill:#fff,stroke:#666
  style w3  fill:#fff,stroke:#666
```

## Preparing the cluster, once {background-image="assets/slide-frame.png" background-size="1500px" background-color="white"}

:::{.sample-medium}
```r
repo <- "https://databricks.packagemanager.posit.co/cran/__linux__/noble/latest"

r_libs <- libraries(
  lib_cran("reticulate", repo = repo),
  lib_cran("tidymodels", repo = repo),
  lib_cran("xgboost", repo = repo),
  lib_cran("readmission", repo = repo)
)

db_libs_install(cluster_id, r_libs)

py_lib <- lib_pypi("rpy2==3.5.7") |>
  libraries()

db_libs_install(cluster_id, py_lib)

wait_for_lib_installs(cluster_id)
```
:::

- Scripted with `brickster`, or done by hand in the cluster's Libraries tab

## What the numbers say {background-image="assets/slide-frame.png" background-size="1500px" background-color="white"}

- **32x faster** than the same job on Posit Workbench, **4x faster** than the best laptop

- The cluster turns an overnight job, or a coffee break job, into a job you wait for

- Concurrency is a dial: 10 workers gave 5 minutes, 32 gave 2.8

- Faster tuning means larger grids, which means better models

# Knowing the limits {background-image="assets/slide-frame-dark.png" background-size="1500px" background-color="#2a7070"}

:::{.dark-slide}
What this is, and what it is not
:::

## Limitations {background-image="assets/slide-frame.png" background-size="1500px" background-color="white"}

- The goal is to **speed up the search**, not to process big data. The data still has to fit in memory

- Results can differ slightly from local runs, because the OS, the R version and the package versions differ

- Downloading predictions roughly doubles the data moved across the wire

- If your data is larger than local memory, use Spark ML instead
